title: X Feed Digest

summary.html: OpenAI’s biggest story in this batch was productization, not just a model bump: the feed treated GPT-5.5 and Codex as a broader shift toward agents that can use your computer, retain more context, and stay active across longer workflows.

summary: Anthropic’s answer was speed and distribution: Claude Code got a web/mobile refresh, while Cat Wu’s interview reinforced that serious AI product teams are now shipping in days instead of quarters.

Open and local models kept gaining credibility. DeepSeek V4 and Qwen3.6 were repeatedly cited as proof that useful agent workflows can run far cheaper, and sometimes fully locally, than many people still assume.
The market conversation widened beyond GPUs: Intel’s quarter was read as evidence that AI inference is also creating demand for CPUs, packaging, and foundry capacity, not just accelerator cards.

items.title: @gdb: OpenAI Pushes Codex Toward Real Agents
items.body: OpenAI framed this week as a move toward more useful agents, with Codex now able to do more on the user’s computer, remember more context, and keep longer-running work going independently. The important signal is that the competition is shifting from raw answer quality toward durable workflow automation.

items.title: @OpenAIDevs: GPT-5.5 Rolls Into Copilot And Foundry
items.body: OpenAI boosted Satya Nadella’s note that GPT-5.5 is rolling out across GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, and Azure Foundry. That makes this look less like an isolated model launch and more like a coordinated enterprise distribution push.

items.title: @ClaudeDevs: Claude Code Expands Across Web And Mobile
items.body: Anthropic refreshed Claude Code on the web and mobile with a new UI, better speed and reliability, and tighter continuity across web, mobile, and CLI. The broader takeaway is that Claude Code is becoming a persistent multi-surface workspace instead of a terminal-only power tool.

items.title: @manateelazycat: Easy Fix For Full 1M DeepSeek Context In Claude Code
items.body: A genuinely useful workflow tip: when routing DeepSeek V4 Flash through Claude Code, appending `[1M]` to the model name exposes the full 1M context window instead of only showing 200K. Small config details like this can materially change whether long-context agent workflows feel practical.

items.title: @julien_c: Local Qwen On A MacBook Pro Feels Much Closer Than Expected
items.body: One of the stronger hands-on posts showed Qwen3.6 27B running locally via llama.cpp inside Pi Coding Agent on a MacBook Pro, with performance described as surprisingly close to recent frontier coding models on real Hugging Face work. If that generalizes, local/private agent stacks are getting serious fast.

items.title: @0xSero: DeepSeek V4 Flash Looks Viable As A Local Frontier Model
items.body: A concrete benchmark post claimed DeepSeek V4 Flash can run uncompressed on four RTX 6000s with sub-second first-token latency, 400K context, and enough throughput for multiple concurrent sessions. The bigger point is that ‘local frontier’ is becoming a realistic category for well-equipped workstations.

items.title: @chenreason: Intel’s Quarter Reframed The AI Bottleneck
items.body: The sharpest market read on the batch argued Intel’s surprise was really about margin and CPU scarcity, not just EPS, with AI inference and agent workloads pulling through more host compute demand alongside GPUs. If that read holds, the AI trade is broadening from accelerators into CPUs, packaging, and foundry capacity.

items.title: @BTCdayu: Value Intel As Two Different Businesses
items.body: A longer deep-dive argued that Intel should be split mentally into a mature CPU cash-flow machine and a strategically protected U.S. foundry option, because those two pieces have very different economics and risk profiles. The useful framing is not just whether Intel is cheap, but which side of the story you are actually underwriting.

items.title: @APompliano: AI Still Looks Expansionary For Jobs
items.body: Pompliano reversed his earlier view that AI would first wipe out junior jobs, pointing instead to stronger hiring data, lower college-grad unemployment, and LinkedIn job-post growth tied to AI roles. Whether or not you buy the full bull case, the labor-market evidence in the feed still looked more additive than purely replacement-driven.

items.title: @lennysan: Cat Wu’s Playbook For Shipping AI Products Faster
items.body: The strongest product thread in the batch argued that Anthropic’s speed comes from small teams shipping research previews, minimizing approvals, and treating product taste as more valuable than rigid role boundaries. It is a useful blueprint for builders: prototype ahead of the models, learn quickly, and remove old scaffolding as capabilities improve.

items.title: @0xEvieYang: Vibe Coding Gets You The Demo, Not The Product
items.body: A concise but accurate reminder from the feed: AI can get you to a 70-point demo in a few hours, but the last 20 points needed to make something feel like a real product still demand much more judgment, domain knowledge, and data. That is the cleanest correction to the current overhyped vibe-coding narrative.

items.title: @Yuchenj_UW: Model Progress Still Comes From Systems Ingenuity
items.body: A smart observation from the DeepSeek discourse was that DeepSeek, Kimi, and Qwen keep finding ways to train strong models under tighter compute constraints by improving architecture and efficiency instead of only spending more GPUs. The strategic implication is that model progress is still being driven by systems creativity, not just capex.
